chapters.title: Chapter 5: Using History Without Being Fooled by It

lessons.title: This Time Is Different: Usually Wrong, Sometimes Right

body.text: "This time is different" is usually right about the world and wrong about the price. The railways, the internet and India's reforms really did change everything. What they never changed was the rule that paying any price for a true story ends badly.

children.text: The legendary investor John Templeton is widely credited with calling "this time it's different" the most dangerous words in investing, and economists Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff used "This Time Is Different" as the title of their 2009 history of eight centuries of financial crises. Every mania in this course came with its version. But a lazy rule of "nothing ever changes" is also expensive. Some things genuinely do change, and investors who ignored them missed some of the greatest opportunities in Indian market history. This lesson helps you tell the two apart.
Three Centuries of "This Time Is Different"

body.caption: The claim, and what actually happened

cells: London, 1720
Converting national debt into company shares creates wealth for everyone
Financial innovation was real
The company lent money to buy its own shares, and the price fell more than 80%
Britain, 1840s
Railways will pay dividends forever
Railways transformed the economy
Too many lines, part-paid shares and rising rates ruined investors
A New Era of electricity, cars and mass consumption has ended the old boom and bust
The technologies were genuinely revolutionary
Margin debt and policy errors turned a crash into an 89% fall
The Nifty Fifty are one-decision stocks, safe at any price
Many were excellent companies
Inflation crushed P/E multiples, and some leaders lost their edge
Japan, 1989
Japanese land never falls in price, and Japan Inc. will dominate the world
Japan was a manufacturing powerhouse
The Nikkei took 34 years to regain its peak
Global and India, 1999
In the new economy, profits and valuations do not matter, only eyeballs and growth
The internet changed everything
Most dot-com and ICE stocks collapsed, even as a few winners went on to dominate
India, 2007
India has decoupled from the US, and the India growth story makes any price fair
India was growing above 9% a year
The Sensex fell about 64% in ten months
India, 2023 to 2024
Domestic SIP money will always support the market, and listing gains are almost guaranteed
Domestic flows really had changed the market
Heavy F&O losses, SME IPO frenzies and a sharp small cap correction followed

body.label: The most famous "different" call in history
body.context: Irving Fisher, one of the most respected economists in America, said stock prices had reached what looked like a permanently high plateau just days before the October 1929 crash. The Dow then fell about 89% by 1932. Brilliance does not protect anyone from the narrative of their own era.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: In October 1929, economist Irving Fisher said stock prices had reached what looked like a permanently high ___.
body.explanation: The phrase "permanently high plateau" has become shorthand for the belief that a boom has broken free of the cycle. Note that Fisher was right about many things in economics. Being an expert does not make anyone immune to euphoria.

children.text: Why the Story Is So Convincing

markDefs.definition: The tendency to give too much weight to recent experience and assume it will continue. Someone who started investing in 2021 may assume markets always recover within months.
The tendency to explain events with a simple, satisfying story, and to believe the story more strongly because it is coherent, even when evidence is thin.

children.text: These claims are persuasive for three reasons. There is always a real change underneath, so the story passes the common sense test. Rising prices appear to confirm it, so every month of gains feels like evidence. And two well-documented biases do the rest:
makes the last few years feel like the permanent state of the world, and the

makes a clean story feel like proof. Add social proof, when colleagues, relatives and financial channels all agree, and doubting the story starts to feel foolish, which is exactly when it is most useful to doubt it.

Now the other side. Refusing to believe anything can change has its own long record of costly mistakes. The changes that turned out to be real usually share a feature: they changed the structure of an economy, a market or its rules, rather than simply justifying higher prices for the same thing.

body.caption: Times when "this time is different" was largely right

cells: India's 1991 reforms
Indian growth and markets will stay slow, controlled and dominated by a few families
The Sensex went from about 1,000 in 1990 to above 80,000 in 2024, through many cycles, as the economy was transformed
Deposit insurance and lenders of last resort
Bank runs are a permanent feature of finance
Systemic runs of the 1930s kind became rare in countries with deposit insurance, though individual bank failures still happen
NSE, screen trading and demat in India
Bad deliveries, forged certificates and opaque prices are just how Indian markets work
They became history within a few years of 1994 to 1996
Negative interest rates
Interest rates cannot fall below zero
The ECB, Japan and Switzerland all ran negative policy rates for years in the 2010s
The internet's biggest winners
The dot-com crash proves the internet was hype
A handful of survivors, including some that fell more than 90% in 2000 to 2001, became among the largest companies on earth
Domestic flows in India
Indian markets always crash when FIIs sell
In 2022, FPIs sold about ₹1.2 lakh crore of shares and the Nifty still ended the year up about 4%
Public sector companies
PSU stocks are permanent value traps
After bad loan clean-ups and a capex push, many PSU stocks were among the market's best performers from 2022 to 2024

body.text: Notice that the internet row contains both lessons at once. The internet really was different, and even many of the companies that later dominated it fell more than 90% in 2000 to 2001. Investors who bought them at the 1999 peak needed years just to break even. Being right about the change and wrong about the price can still cost you a decade.

body.title: Right Story, Wrong Price
body.prompt: A company that goes on to become a genuine winner of a technology revolution falls 94% from its bubble peak before its business takes off. What percentage gain does it need from the bottom just to get back to that peak? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: After a 94% fall, ₹100 becomes ₹6. Gain needed = 100 ÷ 6 − 1 ≈ 15.67, or about 1,567%. The price has to rise almost seventeen times just to break even. Using the recovery formula from Lesson 1.1: 1 ÷ (1 − 0.94) − 1. A great business bought at a manic price can take many years to repay its peak buyers.

columns.label: Usually a warning sign
points: The claim is used to justify paying any price
It says old measures like earnings, cash flow or P/E no longer matter
It relies on prices continuing to rise to work
It arrives with rising leverage, record IPOs and new thematic funds
It cannot be proven wrong by any evidence you can name

columns.label: More likely a genuine change
points: It changes rules, institutions or the structure of the economy
It can be tested: you can name what would prove it wrong
Evidence accumulates in earnings, flows or behaviour, not just prices
It is often doubted and unpopular when it begins
It still has to be bought at a sensible price to be a good investment

body.title: Genuine Change or Warning Sign?
body.question: Which of these claims about Indian markets describes a genuine structural change rather than a "this time is different" warning sign?
options: Real estate in India's big cities can never fall in value
Screen-based trading and dematerialised shares have practically ended the bad deliveries and forged certificates of the 1980s
Every IPO lists at a premium, so applying to all of them is a safe strategy
Valuations no longer matter because SIP money arrives every month
body.explanation: Electronic trading and depositories changed the market's plumbing, and the evidence is plain: forged and lost share certificates are no longer a routine risk. The other claims all use a real trend to justify ignoring price or risk. Indian real estate stagnated in real terms for much of the 2010s, many IPOs list below their issue price, and the Nifty fell 17% from its 2024 peak despite record SIP inflows.

body.title: Five Questions for Any "This Time Is Different" Story
steps: Is this a claim about the economy or technology, or a claim about the price? Judge them separately
Does the argument only work if prices keep rising, or if nothing goes wrong?
What specific evidence would prove the story wrong, and is anyone looking for it?
Who benefits from me believing it: a fund launch, a broker, a promoter, a finfluencer?
If the story is true, what is a sensible price to pay, and is today's price close to it?

body.title: Two Opposite "Different" Claims
body.scenario: At a team lunch in Bengaluru, two colleagues argue about a new technology such as generative AI. One says: "This changes everything. Global AI stocks can't be overvalued at any price, and I'm putting all my savings into them." The other says: "AI will make Indian IT services companies obsolete. I'm selling every IT stock and fund I own today."
body.prompt: Apply this lesson to both claims. What is each person getting right, and what is each missing?
body.modelAnswer: Both colleagues are making a "this time is different" claim, in opposite directions, and both may be right about the change while being careless about price. The first colleague may be right that the technology is transformative, just as railways and the internet were. But "can't be overvalued at any price" is the classic warning sign from this lesson: it dismisses valuation, relies on prices continuing to rise, and puts all savings into one theme, exactly the setup of 1845, 1999 and 2007. Even the eventual winners of the internet fell more than 90% after 1999. The second colleague may be right that the technology will disrupt parts of IT services, but "obsolete" and "sell everything today" treat a possible change as certain and immediate. Indian IT companies survived and adapted through Y2K, the dot-com bust, cloud computing and automation, and a large part of any disruption risk may already be reflected in their prices. For both, the useful questions are the same: what evidence in earnings and business results would confirm or refute the story, what price already assumes the story is true, and how much of a portfolio should any single theme represent? A sensible approach is to keep a diversified core, size any thematic bet modestly, and update as evidence arrives rather than acting on the narrative alone.

cards.definition: The belief that the old rules of valuation and cycles no longer apply because of a new development. Usually wrong about prices, sometimes right about the underlying change.
Irving Fisher's October 1929 description of US stock prices, days before the crash. A byword for boom-era overconfidence.
Overweighting recent experience and assuming it will continue.
Believing a simple, coherent story more than the evidence justifies.
A lasting change in an economy's rules, institutions or makeup, such as India's 1991 reforms or dematerialised shares, as opposed to a reason to pay higher prices for the same thing.
Correctly identifying a transformative change but paying so much that returns are poor for years.

children.text: You now have a long view of market history, a set of cycle engines, a valuation dashboard and a filter for new-era stories. The final lesson turns all of it into something you can actually use: a cycle-aware investing mindset built for real Indian investors, with a plan you can follow when the next boom or bust arrives.

body.text: Historical claims, quotations and figures in this lesson are summarised from widely reported sources and are approximate. References to technologies, sectors and companies are for education only and are not forecasts or recommendations to buy or sell any security. Nothing here is investment advice.

points: Every mania in this course came with a "this time is different" story, from the South Sea Company in 1720 to decoupling in 2007 and guaranteed listing gains in 2024
These stories persuade because there is always a real change underneath, rising prices seem to confirm them, and recency bias and the narrative fallacy do the rest
Sometimes it really is different: India's 1991 reforms, demat and screen trading, deposit insurance, negative rates and domestic flows all proved the sceptics wrong
Genuine changes alter rules, institutions or economic structure and can be tested, while warning signs dismiss valuation and rely on prices rising
Being right about a change and wrong about the price can still be ruinous: a 94% fall needs a gain of about 1,567% to recover
Judge the story and the price separately, name what would prove the story wrong, and size any thematic bet modestly
